entries_new.name: Paulet affair (British occupation of Hawaii, 1843)
entries_new.stopped_by: Rear-Admiral Richard Thomas, with US warships present
entries_new.challenge: Hawaiian government; American naval officers; the British Admiralty
entries_new.mechanism: A naval captain acting without orders from London forced a cession of disputed land and ran the government under a commission.
entries_new.story: In February 1843 Captain Lord George Paulet of the Royal Navy ship HMS Carysfort sailed into Honolulu and demanded that King Kamehameha III meet him, backing a dispute about land claimed by the British consul Richard Charlton. Under threat of attack the Hawaiian government signed over the disputed land under protest on 25 February. Paulet set up a commission of himself and three others as government and raised the British flag. London had not authorised this. Rear-Admiral Richard Thomas arrived on 26 July and ended the occupation on 31 July 1843, after American warships had also reached Honolulu. The date is now a Hawaiian holiday.

entries_new.name: William Astor Chanler's 1902 Venezuela insurrection
entries_new.stopped_by: Called off after Castro agreed to honour his loan terms
entries_new.challenge: Government of Venezuela under Cipriano Castro
entries_new.mechanism: Foreign creditors paid for an armed landing meant to force or replace a debtor government.
entries_new.story: In 1902 Dutch investors who feared that Venezuelan President Cipriano Castro would default on a large loan approached the American former congressman William Astor Chanler and asked him to stage a rebellion. According to his Wikipedia biography, he raised a small army of adventurers, which landed on the Venezuelan coast and marched inland. The rising was called off when Castro agreed to comply with the terms of his loans. Chanler later borrowed funds for a water and sewage project in Tampico, Mexico, and published a fictionalised account of the episode in 1921 under the pen name John Brent.

entries_new.name: Chatham Roberdeau Wheat's expeditions
entries_new.mechanism: Private soldier-for-hire commanding volunteers in other countries' conflicts.
entries_new.story: Chatham Roberdeau Wheat was a Louisiana lawyer and legislator who, after the Mexican-American War, served as a fighter for hire in several foreign campaigns. He held a colonel's commission from Narciso Lopez in the Cuban filibustering expeditions (private armies raised in the United States to invade a foreign country). In 1855 the State of Guerrero in Mexico made him a brigadier general of artillery in the campaign of Juan Alvarez against Santa Anna. He then went to Italy to serve under Garibaldi but left when Virginia seceded. He raised the Louisiana Tigers battalion for the Confederacy and died in June 1862.

entries_new.name: Aunus expedition (Finnish volunteers in Olonets Karelia)
entries_new.founder: Gunnar von Hertzen, later Aarne Sihvo
entries_new.stopped_by: Soviet Red Army and Red Guard counterattack; Treaty of Tartu border
entries_new.challenge: Soviet Russia
entries_new.mechanism: Volunteer army seeking to occupy a neighbouring region and attach it to Finland.
entries_new.story: In April 1919 about a thousand Finnish volunteers crossed into Olonets Karelia, which Finns call Aunus, a Russian-ruled area inhabited mostly by Finnic-language people. The aims were Lodeynoye Pole, Petrozavodsk and the Murmansk railway. A second recruitment of 2,000 volunteers followed, but few local Karelians joined. A Red Army landing at Vitele on 26 June forced the Finns back. Under the 1920 Treaty of Tartu the border was drawn with Repola and Porajarvi on the Soviet side, and Finnish troops left by February 1921. The expedition was one of several Finnish 'kinship wars' of the period.

entries_new.name: Falke expedition (Cumana landing, 1929)
entries_new.challenge: Government of Juan Vicente Gomez
entries_new.mechanism: Exile junta tried to land an armed force from a ship to overthrow a dictator.
entries_new.story: On 11 August 1929 the steamship Falke, renamed General Anzoategui for the occasion, entered the Venezuelan port of Cumana carrying 250 to 300 men led by the former admiral Roman Delgado Chalbaud. Exiles in Paris had formed a Junta de Liberacion Nacional to oust President Juan Vicente Gomez. Venezuelan forces met the ship. Delgado was killed on the first day, and the expedition's leaders surrendered on 24 August. His son Carlos escaped. The Venezuelan envoy in Europe, Jose Ignacio Cardenas, had reported the plan, which helped defeat it.

entries_new.name: Northern Autonomous Zone of Junbish-e Milli
entries_new.stopped_by: Taliban capture in 1998; later absorbed into the Afghan state
entries_new.challenge: Rival Afghan factions, the Taliban, and later the central government
entries_new.mechanism: A former army division kept its territory when the national government collapsed.
entries_new.story: From 1992 the Uzbek-led Junbish-e Milli movement under Abdul Rashid Dostum held seven provinces of northern Afghanistan around Mazar-e-Sharif, with about five million people according to Wikipedia. It had its own airline, Balkh Airlines, printed its own currency, had a foreign minister and drew electricity from Uzbekistan. The Taliban took Mazar-e-Sharif in August 1998 and Dostum fled. He returned in 2001 and the zone became part of the new Islamic Republic of Afghanistan in law while he kept control in practice. The last report that he controlled the city is dated 4 November 2007.

entries_new.name: Tocoron prison and Tren de Aragua
entries_new.founder: Hector Rusthenford Guerrero Flores and others
entries_new.challenge: Venezuelan security forces; US executive designation and court challenges
entries_new.mechanism: A prison run from inside by a criminal group served as its base.
entries_new.story: Tren de Aragua is a Venezuelan criminal group that Wikipedia says began inside the Tocoron prison in Aragua state, where its leader Hector Guerrero Flores was held from 2013 to 2023. The prison served as the group's de facto headquarters until Venezuelan security forces took it over in a 2023 raid, after which the leadership escaped. In February 2025 the United States designated the group a Foreign Terrorist Organization and cited the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 for deportations; that order was challenged in court, and some experts dispute the terrorist label, describing the group as money-driven. Guerrero is reported to have died in June 2026.

entries_new.name: Pailin, Khmer Rouge stronghold
entries_new.stopped_by: Surrender of the Ieng Sary faction in 1996; integration under the Cambodian government
entries_new.challenge: Government of Cambodia
entries_new.mechanism: A retreating movement held a resource-rich border district funded by gem and timber extraction.
entries_new.story: Pailin, a gem-mining district in western Cambodia near the Thai border, was captured by the Khmer Rouge on 20 April 1975. After Vietnamese forces ousted the Khmer Rouge in 1979 the movement retreated there, and Wikipedia says it held the area long afterwards and used it as the capital of its Provisional Government of National Union and National Salvation of Cambodia from 1994 to 1998. The Ieng Sary faction surrendered in 1996, and Pailin was separated from Battambang province. Prime Minister Hun Sen's government let former members manage it as a special administrative area to keep the peace.

entries_new.name: Sheng Shicai's rule of Xinjiang
entries_new.stopped_by: Removal by the Chinese national government in August 1944
entries_new.challenge: Ma Zhongying, Zhang Peiyuan, the Chinese national government
entries_new.mechanism: A provincial commander held power by a Soviet military alliance, then tried to switch patrons.
entries_new.story: Sheng Shicai became military governor of Xinjiang after a coup on 12 April 1933 and ruled until August 1944. He defeated rivals Ma Zhongying and Zhang Peiyuan by June 1934 after inviting Soviet troops to intervene, and in return subordinated the province to Moscow; the Soviets held a monopoly on Xinjiang trade and extracted oil and rare materials. Wikipedia reports a purge in 1937 that executed, tortured to death or imprisoned 100,000 people. He expelled Soviet personnel in July 1942, tried to switch sides again in 1944, and was removed by the Chinese government, which made him a minister.

entries_new.name: Ismail Khan's Herat (the "Emir of Herat")
entries_new.stopped_by: Removal by President Karzai and pressure from rival commanders, March 2004
entries_new.challenge: Afghan Transitional Administration under Hamid Karzai
entries_new.mechanism: A provincial governor kept customs revenue and an armed force outside central control.
entries_new.story: After the Taliban fell in December 2001, Ismail Khan, a former mujahideen commander, again became governor of Herat in western Afghanistan. Wikipedia reports that he took control of the city from the local religious scholars, held the trade route to Iran as a main source of revenue, and was called Emir of Herat. He paid government employees and invested in public services, though he was accused of human rights abuses and of ruling like a private fiefdom. He refused to pass customs revenue from Iran and Turkmenistan to the national government. President Karzai removed him from his army command in August 2003, and rival commanders and the central government forced him out in March 2004.

entries_new.name: Kuomintang army in the Shan States of Burma
entries_new.stopped_by: Burmese and Chinese operations in 1960 and 1961; evacuation to Taiwan
entries_new.challenge: Government of Burma; People's Republic of China; United Nations pressure
entries_new.mechanism: A displaced army held border hills with outside supply and opium revenue.
entries_new.story: In late 1949 and early 1950 troops of the Republic of China army under Lieutenant-General Li Mi crossed from Yunnan into Burma after losing the Chinese Civil War. They made several raids into Yunnan, were pushed back each time, and from late 1952 spread out across the Shan States and part of Kachin State. The area became Burma's main opium-producing region, and the troops took part in the opium trade, according to Wikipedia. Burma appealed to the United Nations in 1953. Li Mi announced the army's dissolution on 30 May 1954, but about 6,000 irregulars stayed until Burmese and Chinese operations in 1960 and 1961.

entries_new.name: Tambov Rebellion and Antonov's peasant army
entries_new.challenge: Soviet Russian government
entries_new.mechanism: Peasants replaced local Soviet authority with their own union and armed bands.
entries_new.story: Beginning in August 1920 peasants in Tambov governorate, about 500 km southeast of Moscow, resisted forced grain requisitions. Led by Alexander Antonov, a Left Socialist-Revolutionary, and organised through the Union of Working Peasants, they abolished Soviet institutions in the areas they held. By October 1920 the Bolsheviks controlled little of the countryside beyond Tambov city. In May 1921 a Red Army force of 50,000 to 100,000 under Tukhachevsky moved in, and on 12 June 1921 chemical weapons use against rebels in forests was authorised. Antonov was killed on 24 June 1922. Wikipedia cites estimates of about 100,000 arrested and 15,000 killed.

entries_new.name: Republic of Uzice
entries_new.challenge: German occupation forces
entries_new.mechanism: Partisans took a liberated district and ran it with people's councils.
entries_new.story: In autumn 1941, in German-occupied Yugoslavia, Partisan resistance fighters held a stretch of western Serbia centred on the town of Uzice, between the Drina and Zapadna Morava rivers. Wikipedia gives its population as over 300,000 (another source says nearly one million) and its area as 15,000 or 20,000 square kilometres. It was run by local people's councils and had schools, a newspaper called Borba, a postal system, about 145 km of railway and an ammunition factory in the vaults under a bank. German troops retook the area in the First anti-Partisan offensive in November 1941, and the Partisans moved to Bosnia in early December.

entries_new.name: Labin Republic (Albona Republic)
entries_new.founder: Striking miners led by Giovanni Pippan, Giacomo Macillis and Lelio Zustovich
entries_new.challenge: Italian government and mine owners (Societa Anonima Carbonifera Arsa)
entries_new.mechanism: Miners occupied the workplace and proclaimed self-government.
entries_new.story: On 7 March 1921, during a strike by about two thousand miners at the Arsa coal mines in Labin, in Istria (then newly annexed by Italy), the miners occupied the mines and proclaimed a republic under the slogan 'Kova je nasa' (the mine is ours). The strike followed attacks by fascists on a union in Trieste and the beating of the strike leader Giovanni Pippan. Miners formed a red guard and ran production themselves with some farmers' support. On 8 April Italian authorities sent a thousand soldiers at the owners' request and ended it. Fifty-two miners were indicted and a jury acquitted them.

entries_new.name: Sarbadar state of Sabzavar
entries_new.currency: Coins minted, first in the name of Togha Temur
entries_new.challenge: Ilkhanid claimants, Togha Temur, Chobanids, Timur
entries_new.mechanism: A local rising took towns and ruled by rotating leaders under nominal overlords.
entries_new.story: The Sarbadars (Persian for 'head on gallows') ruled part of western Khurasan from 1337, as the Mongol Ilkhanate broke up, with their capital at Sabzavar. Their rulers were a mix of secular leaders and dervishes (members of a mystic religious order), who sometimes shared power and often fell out. Wikipedia describes the government as something like an oligarchy or republic with no dynastic line, and none of the rulers claimed legitimate sovereignty. They sometimes accepted Mongol claimants as overlord for convenience. About 1340 they defeated the Ja'un Qurban and the khan Togha Temur and took Gurgan. The last ruler, Khwaja Ali Mu'ayyad, submitted to Timur in 1381.

entries_new.name: Second Servile War in Sicily
entries_new.challenge: Roman Republic
entries_new.mechanism: Rebel slave kings held fortified towns using captured Roman arms.
entries_new.story: From 104 to 100 BC enslaved people on Sicily rose against the Roman Republic. The trigger was an order that slaves from Rome's allies be freed: the governor Publius Licinius Nerva freed about 800 people, then revoked it. A former slave called Salvius, who took the name Tryphon, defeated Roman forces, took Morgantina and led an army reported at 2,000 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers. Athenion, a Cilician slave, led a second rising in the west and later succeeded Salvius as king. The consul Manius Aquillius defeated Athenion in 101 BC. Wikipedia says 1,000 survivors were sent to the Rome arena and killed each other instead of fighting.

entries_new.name: Overthrow and annexation of Hawaii, 1893 to 1898
entries_new.challenge: Queen Liliuokalani; the Blount investigation; Hawaiian sovereignty movement
entries_new.mechanism: A coup backed by US naval personnel was followed by annexation through a joint resolution of Congress.
entries_new.story: On 17 January 1893 a Committee of Safety of foreign-born and Hawaiian-born residents of Honolulu overthrew Queen Liliuokalani. The kingdom had no army, and the committee asked the US minister John L. Stevens to land Marines and sailors, which he did. The committee set up the Republic of Hawaii, aiming at annexation. President Cleveland sent James Blount to investigate; his July 1893 report said US diplomats and troops were responsible for the change. A Senate committee under John Tyler Morgan reached a contrary view. President McKinley signed the Newlands Resolution, and annexation took effect on 7 July 1898. A 1993 US Apology Resolution acknowledged US participation.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom

entries_new.name: Anschluss: annexation of Austria by Germany, 1938
entries_new.challenge: Austrian chancellor Schuschnigg; Mexican delegate at the League of Nations; Allied Moscow Declaration
entries_new.mechanism: Threat of invasion forced a change of government, then a law of union and a plebiscite.
entries_new.story: On 12 March 1938 German troops crossed into Austria, after Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg had been pressed to resign and the Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart installed in his place. Schuschnigg had called a referendum on Austrian independence for 13 March, which Hitler demanded be cancelled. A law of 13 March made Austria a province called Ostmark, and a controlled plebiscite on 10 April officially recorded 99.7 percent support. On 18 March Germany told the League of Nations; Mexico's delegate protested. The Moscow Declaration of 1943 by the US, Soviet Union and UK later treated the annexation as null.

entries_new.name: Argentine invasion of the Falkland Islands, 1982
entries_new.challenge: United Kingdom; UN Security Council Resolution 502
entries_new.mechanism: Armed seizure of a territory over which two states claim sovereignty.
entries_new.story: On 2 April 1982 Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, and the next day South Georgia, describing the action as reclaiming its own territory. The United Kingdom, which has held the islands as a Crown colony since 1841, called it an invasion. UN Security Council Resolution 502, adopted 10 to 1 with four abstentions, called for the withdrawal of Argentine forces and avoided the sovereignty question. A British task force arrived, and Argentina surrendered on 14 June after 74 days. The war killed 649 Argentine and 255 British military personnel and 3 islanders. Argentina's 1994 constitution declares the islands part of one of its provinces.

entries_new.name: Chinese annexation of Central Tibet, 1950 to 1951
entries_new.challenge: Tibetan government, then the Dalai Lama from 1959; Central Tibetan Administration
entries_new.mechanism: Military advance followed by a treaty signed in Beijing.
entries_new.story: After the fall of the Qing dynasty, central Tibet governed itself, and by 1917 was de facto independent. The People's Liberation Army crossed the Jinsha River on 6 or 7 October 1950 and had taken Chamdo by 19 October. Tibetan negotiators in Beijing were given a finished text, the Seventeen Point Agreement, and signed it on 23 May 1951 without permission from Lhasa to do so, according to Wikipedia. The Dalai Lama accepted it in October 1951. He fled in 1959 and repudiated it, saying he approved it under duress. China calls the event 'Peaceful Liberation'; the exiled administration calls it an invasion.

entries_new.name: Security Council Resolution 242
entries_new.mechanism: A Security Council text that rejects keeping territory taken in war and ties withdrawal to recognised borders.
entries_new.story: Resolution 242 was adopted unanimously by the UN Security Council on 22 November 1967, after the Six-Day War. Its preamble refers to the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war. It calls for a just and lasting peace that includes withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict and respect for the sovereignty and secure, recognised boundaries of every state in the area. It was passed under Chapter VI of the Charter, which covers peaceful settlement. Syria accepted it conditionally in 1972. Wikipedia describes it as the basis of later talks and of the Israel-Egypt (1979) and Israel-Jordan (1994) peace treaties.

entries_new.name: Security Council Resolution 478
entries_new.challenge: Israel, which rejected it
entries_new.mechanism: A Council decision that an annexation law is void and should not be recognised by other states.
entries_new.story: Resolution 478, adopted on 20 August 1980 by 14 votes to none with the United States abstaining, is the last of seven Security Council resolutions condemning Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem. It condemned the 1980 Jerusalem Law, which declared Jerusalem Israel's complete and united capital, as a violation of international law, and said the Council would not recognise it. It called on member states to withdraw diplomatic missions from the city. Israel rejected the resolution. The US representative called the instruction on embassies not binding. It was not adopted under Chapter VII, though the UN treats findings of illegal situations as binding.

entries_new.name: M23 (AFC-M23) areas of North and South Kivu
entries_new.challenge: Congolese government and army (FARDC); UN peacekeepers; UN Security Council sanctions
entries_new.mechanism: An armed group holding towns and mining areas and running a parallel administration over them.
entries_new.story: The March 23 Movement (M23) was formed in May 2012 by former fighters of the CNDP who had mutinied against the Congolese army. It took Goma, capital of North Kivu, on 20 November 2012, and withdrew after Great Lakes regional pressure; a UN report found Rwanda created and commanded it then. After a renewed offensive from 2022, M23 announced the capture of Goma on 27 January 2025 and of Bukavu on 16 February 2025. In Rubaya it set up a mineral ministry that taxed coltan and issued permits to miners and traders. The DRC and Rwanda signed a peace agreement in Washington on 27 June 2025.

entries_new.name: Ansaru in north-west Nigeria
aka: Vanguard for the Protection of Muslims in Black Africa
entries_new.founder: Khalid Barnawi and Abubakar Adam Kambar
entries_new.challenge: Nigerian government and military
entries_new.mechanism: A militant group using forest camps in a region with existing armed banditry.
entries_new.story: Ansaru is a Nigerian jihadist group that split from Boko Haram and announced in 2012 that it was independent and pledged to al-Qaeda. Wikipedia says it operated around Kano State, carried out kidnappings of foreigners, and stopped activity in 2013 after commanders returned to Boko Haram. It reappeared in 2020. The article says it maintains a presence in Kaduna State local government areas such as Birnin Gwari, Chikun, Igabi and Giwa. The Nigerian military reported attacks on camps linked to the group in February and August 2020. It states an aim of reviving the Sokoto Caliphate.

entries_new.name: General Assembly Resolution 3314, Definition of Aggression
entries_new.mechanism: A General Assembly definition of which state acts count as aggression, including annexation by force.
entries_new.story: Resolution 3314 (XXIX) was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 14 December 1974 as a non-binding recommendation to the Security Council. It separates an act of aggression, which makes a state internationally responsible, from a war of aggression, which is a crime against international peace. Article 3 lists armed invasion or attack, occupation and annexation by force, bombardment, blockade and attacks on another state's armed forces as acts of aggression. It also covers a state allowing others to use its territory for aggression and sending armed irregulars or mercenaries. Critics call its rules on irregulars vague and say it treats only states as responsible parties.

entries_new.name: Sokoto Caliphate
entries_new.stopped_by: British, French and German conquest in 1903
entries_new.challenge: Hausa kingdoms; later European colonial forces
entries_new.mechanism: A religious reform movement conquered neighbouring kingdoms and ruled them as emirates under one caliph.
entries_new.story: The Sokoto Caliphate was a Sunni Muslim state in West Africa founded by Usman dan Fodio in 1804, in the Fulani jihads against the Hausa kingdoms. His followers pledged allegiance to him as Commander of the Faithful after the Hausa king Yunfa attempted to kill him in 1802. By 1808 it controlled Hausaland and nearby states, and it was a loose confederation of over 30 emirates under the Sultan of Sokoto. Wikipedia estimates 10 to 20 million people by 1837, and at least 1 million and perhaps 2.5 million slaves by 1900. British, French and German forces conquered it in 1903, when the last caliph, Attahiru, was killed. The sultan's title remains.

entries_new.name: Costa Chica of Guerrero, refuge of escaped slaves
entries_new.mechanism: Runaways settled a remote coast and traded labor for the protection of local landholders.
entries_new.story: The Costa Chica is a stretch of Pacific coast in Guerrero, Mexico, running from just south of Acapulco to the Oaxaca border. Wikipedia reports that enslaved Africans who escaped from sugar plantations, mines and ranches elsewhere in colonial Mexico migrated to this isolated region and found refuge. Spanish landholders there gave them protection in return for cheap labor, mostly tending cattle and curing leather. Over time there was significant mixing with Europeans and indigenous people. Today the area has one of Mexico's two main Afro-Mexican populations, concentrated between Marquelia and Cuajinicuilapa, alongside indigenous Amuzgo communities.

entries_new.name: Revolt of Aristonicus (Eumenes III) at Pergamon
entries_new.challenge: Roman Republic and neighbouring Anatolian kingdoms and Greek cities
entries_new.mechanism: A claimant to a bequeathed throne raised a force and offered freedom to slaves and serfs.
entries_new.story: When King Attalus III of Pergamon died in 133 BC he left his kingdom to Rome. Aristonicus, who claimed to be an illegitimate son of the earlier king Eumenes II, took the name Eumenes III and claimed the throne. He seized coastal cities including Samos, Myndus and Colophon and killed the Roman consul Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus. Turning inland, he promised freedom to slaves and serfs, and was joined by the Stoic philosopher Blossius, who planned a state called Heliopolis. The consul Marcus Perpenna defeated him by 129 BC, and he was sent to Rome. How far he was a social revolutionary or a dynastic claimant is uncertain.

entries_new.name: Torre de David (Centro Financiero Confinanzas), Caracas
entries_new.challenge: Government of Venezuela
entries_new.mechanism: Families occupied an abandoned state-held building and ran its services themselves.
entries_new.story: Centro Financiero Confinanzas is an unfinished skyscraper in downtown Caracas whose construction stopped in 1994 during Venezuela's banking crisis. In October 2007 squatters led by ex-convicts occupied it, in a city short of about 400,000 homes. Residents improvised water and electricity, and the tower grew to 700 families, over 2,500 people by 2011, with a peak population of 5,000. Shops, barbershops and an unlicensed dentist operated inside. On 22 July 2014 the government launched 'Operation Zamora 2014' and moved the families to new housing in Cua, finishing by June 2015. The tower stands unfinished.

entries_new.name: Nahr al-Bared refugee camp
entries_new.founder: League of Red Cross Societies, with UNRWA responsible for the old camp
entries_new.challenge: Lebanese Army
entries_new.mechanism: Camp security left to Palestinian factions under the 1969 Cairo Agreement.
entries_new.story: Nahr al-Bared is a Palestinian refugee camp 16 km from Tripoli in northern Lebanon, set up in December 1949 for people displaced in 1948. Under the 1969 Cairo Agreement the Lebanese Army does not conventionally enter such camps and Palestinian factions provide internal security. On 20 May 2007, after a clash in Tripoli, members of the Fatah al-Islam militant group attacked an army checkpoint at the camp, and the army shelled it. Most residents fled, and the last civilians were evacuated on 24 August. The army took full control on 2 September 2007. About 30,000 displaced Palestinians and descendants live in and around the camp.
